WorldMark: A Unified Benchmark Suite for Interactive Video World Models

Xiaojie Xu Affiliation: Alaya Studio, Shanda AI Research Tokyo    Zhengyuan Lin Affiliation: Alaya Studio, Shanda AI Research Tokyo Affiliation: The University of Tokyo    Kang He Affiliation: Alaya Studio, Shanda AI Research Tokyo Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute    Yukang Feng Affiliation: Alaya Studio, Shanda AI Research Tokyo Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute    Xiaofeng Mao Affiliation: Alaya Studio, Shanda AI Research Tokyo    Yuanyang Yin Affiliation: Alaya Studio, Shanda AI Research Tokyo Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute    Kaipeng Zhang† Affiliation: Alaya Studio, Shanda AI Research Tokyo Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute    Yongtao Ge† Affiliation: Alaya Studio, Shanda AI Research Tokyo
Abstract

Interactive video generation models such as Genie, YUME, HY-World, and Matrix-Game are advancing rapidly, yet every model is evaluated on its own benchmark with private scenes and trajectories, making fair cross-model comparison impossible. Existing public benchmarks offer useful metrics such as trajectory error, aesthetic scores, and VLM-based judgments, but none supplies the standardized test conditions—identical scenes, identical action sequences, and a unified control interface—needed to make those metrics comparable across models with heterogeneous inputs. We introduce WorldMark, the first benchmark that provides such a common playing field for interactive Image-to-Video world models. WorldMark contributes: (1) a unified action-mapping layer that translates a shared WASD-style action vocabulary into each model’s native control format, enabling apples-to-apples comparison across six major models on identical scenes and trajectories; (2) a hierarchical test suite of 500 evaluation cases covering first- and third-person viewpoints, photorealistic and stylized scenes, and three difficulty tiers from Easy to Hard spanning 20–60 s; and (3) a modular evaluation toolkit for Visual Quality, Control Alignment, and World Consistency, designed so that researchers can reuse our standardized inputs while plugging in their own metrics as the field evolves. We will release all data, evaluation code, and model outputs to facilitate future research. Beyond offline metrics, we launch World Model Arena (warena.ai), an online platform where anyone can pit leading world models against each other in side-by-side battles and watch the live leaderboard.

1 Introduction

A World Model Ha and Schmidhuber (2018) should not merely synthesize plausible video frames Zhao et al. (2025); Cen et al. (2025); Hassan et al. (2025); Xiao et al. (); it must function as an interactive environment Guo et al. (2025); Team et al. (2025) that responds faithfully to user actions and camera controls while preserving long-term scene memory. Recent months have seen a surge of systems pursuing this goal through heterogeneous control interfaces: YUME 1.5 Mao et al. (2025b); Mao et al. (2025a) accepts WASD keyboard inputs via natural-language captions, HY-World 1.5 Sun et al. (2025) takes structured pose commands, Matrix-Game 2.0 He et al. (2025) exposes custom action functions, and Genie 3 Google DeepMind (2025b), building on the earlier Genie Bruce et al. (2024), maps gamepad-style controls. Yet each of these models publishes results on its own private benchmark with bespoke trajectories and scenes, making it nearly impossible to determine which model truly advances world modeling and which merely excels under favorable test conditions.

Existing public benchmarks do not fill this gap. VBench Huang et al. (2024) and VBench++ Huang and others (2024) comprehensively evaluate text-to-video and image-to-video generation quality, but contain no notion of action control or camera trajectory. WorldScore Duan et al. (2025) introduces 3D-aware consistency metrics via SLAM-based reconstruction, yet its drone-flythrough viewpoints and passive camera paths are a poor proxy for the first-person, action-driven interaction that characterizes world models. The concurrent MIND benchmark Ye et al. (2026) does target interactive generation, but conditions evaluation on ground-truth camera trajectories—a modality that most keyboard-controlled models (YUME, Open-Oasis, Genie) simply cannot accept. Other recent efforts—PhyGenBench Meng et al. (2025), WorldModelBench Li et al. (2025a), and 4DWorldBench Lu et al. (2025)—assess physical plausibility or 3D/4D consistency but likewise lack standardized interactive action sequences for cross-model comparison. In every case, a critical disconnect persists: no benchmark jointly evaluates action controllability, visual quality, and long-horizon world consistency under the interactive paradigm that defines emerging world models. As a result, the strikingly divergent outputs produced by current models under the same reference image and action sequence (Fig. 1(c)) remain invisible to existing evaluation protocols.

We argue that the root cause of this evaluation gap is not a lack of metrics—trajectory error Duan et al. (2025); Ye et al. (2026), aesthetic scores Huang and others (2024), and VLM-based judgments Li et al. (2025a); Meng et al. (2025); Peng et al. (2025) all exist—but rather the absence of standardized test conditions. When every model is evaluated on its own scenes, its own trajectories, and its own action definitions, even identical metrics yield incomparable numbers. What the field needs first is a common playing field: the same scenes, the same action sequences, and a transparent translation layer that feeds each model semantically equivalent inputs through its native control interface.

We address this need with WorldMark, the first standardized benchmark purpose-built for interactive Image-to-Video (I2V) world models (Fig. 1). The design centers on two pillars.

(i) Unified test infrastructure. We define a shared WASD-style action vocabulary and build an action-mapping layer that translates it into each model’s heterogeneous control format—caption-based prompts for YUME Mao et al. (2025a), structured pose parameters for HY-World 1.5 Sun et al. (2025), one-hot action tensors for Open-Oasis Decart et al. (2024), and so on—so that all six evaluated models receive semantically identical instructions on exactly the same scenes. We further curate a hierarchical test suite of 500 cases drawn from 50 reference images spanning first-/third-person perspectives and photorealistic/stylized scenes, with three difficulty tiers: Easy (single-segment, 20 s), Medium (two-segment, 40 s), and Hard (three-segment, 60 s) action sequences ranging from simple forward motion to complex patrol routes and 360∘ rotations. A VLM-based scene-aware filtering step automatically selects physically plausible actions for each image, ensuring that the test suite is both challenging and semantically grounded.

(ii) Default evaluation toolkit. On top of this standardized infrastructure, we provide a ready-to-use metric suite covering three dimensions—Video Quality, Control Alignment, and World Consistency—combining geometric trajectory metrics with VLM-based scoring. Because all models are evaluated on identical inputs, even simple metrics suffice to reveal meaningful cross-model differences. Meanwhile, the open design allows researchers to plug in their own metrics or scoring models as the field matures.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We present WorldMark, the first standardized benchmark for interactive I2V world models. Its core is a unified action mapper and a curated test suite of 500 cases that enable apples-to-apples comparison across six models with heterogeneous control interfaces (YUME 1.5 Mao et al. (2025a), Matrix-Game 2.0 He et al. (2025), HY-World 1.5 Sun et al. (2025), HY-GameCraft Li et al. (2025b); Tang et al. (2025), Open-Oasis Decart et al. (2024), and Genie 3 Google DeepMind (2025b)).

  • •

    We provide a default evaluation toolkit covering Visual Quality, Control Alignment, and World Consistency via both geometric and VLM-based metrics. The toolkit is modular: researchers can reuse our standardized inputs while substituting or extending metrics as needed.

  • •

    We conduct the first systematic cross-model evaluation under controlled conditions, revealing that visual quality and world consistency are largely uncorrelated—the model producing the most aesthetically pleasing frames (YUME 1.5 Mao et al. (2025a)) ranks poorly on long-horizon coherence, while the most geometrically consistent model (Genie 3 Google DeepMind (2025b)) has only moderate visual fidelity—and that the third-person setting remains a pronounced failure mode in which several open-source models lose much of their control precision, providing actionable insights and open data for the community.

2 Related Work

2.1 Interactive Video Models for World Simulation

Video generation has advanced rapidly from early GAN- and VAE-based methods to diffusion architectures Ho et al. (2022); Blattmann et al. (2023) with camera- and motion-controllable extensions He et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2024), and, more recently, to large-scale Video Diffusion Transformers such as Sora Liu et al. (2024), CogVideoX Yang et al. (), HunyuanVideo Kong et al. (2024), and Wan Wan et al. (2025). These breakthroughs in quality and duration have prompted researchers to explore video generation models as interactive world simulators Yang et al. (2024). MineWorld Guo et al. (2025) jointly models discrete visual and action tokens via an autoregressive Transformer, while Open-Oasis Decart et al. (2024) combines a DiT backbone with Diffusion Forcing for frame-by-frame autoregressive generation; both pioneered action-aware real-time interaction within the Minecraft domain, alongside GameNGen Valevski et al. (2024) and DIAMOND Alonso et al. (2024). Matrix-Game 2.0 He et al. (2025) and HY-World 1.5 Sun et al. (2025) subsequently extended interactive generation to photorealistic open worlds through streaming inference and long-horizon geometric consistency, while closed-loop refinement further improves temporal coherence. HY-GameCraft Li et al. (2025b); Tang et al. (2025) achieves fine-grained control through a unified camera representation, YUME 1.5 Mao et al. (2025a) enables event-driven exploration via text-controlled generation, and Genie 3 Google DeepMind (2025b) maps gamepad-style controls to open-ended 3D worlds.

Despite this rapid progress, the evaluation systems for these models remain fragmented: each typically reports results on a private benchmark with its own scenes, trajectories, and metrics—e.g., yume-Bench for YUME Mao et al. (2025a), GameWorld Score for Matrix-Game Zhang et al. (2025), and InterBench for HY-GameCraft-2 Tang et al. (2025). This makes cross-model comparison effectively impossible.

2.2 Evaluation Benchmarks for Video World Models

Evaluation standards for video generation have evolved along multiple axes. VBench Huang et al. (2024) and VBench++ Huang and others (2024) define multi-dimensional quality metrics for text-to-video and image-to-video generation, respectively. PhyGenBench Meng et al. (2025) tests physical common sense across 27 laws, and WorldModelBench Li et al. (2025a) probes world-model rigor by detecting subtle physical violations such as mass conservation. WorldScore Duan et al. (2025) and 4DWorldBench Lu et al. (2025) evaluate scene controllability and consistency through explicit camera trajectories and 3D/4D reconstruction quality. The concurrent MIND benchmark Ye et al. (2026) directly targets interactive world models, assessing memory consistency and action control at 1080p.

Taken together, these benchmarks provide a rich set of metrics—trajectory error, perceptual distance Zhang et al. (2018), video fidelity Unterthiner et al. (2019), aesthetic scores, VLM-based judgments, physical-violation detection—but none provides standardized test conditions for interactive models. Each interactive model still evaluates on its own private scenes and action definitions, so even shared metrics produce incomparable numbers. As shown in Tab. 1, WorldMark addresses this gap by supplying a common set of scenes, action sequences, and a unified control-interface translation layer, so that existing and future metrics can be applied on equal footing across models.

3 WorldMark Suite

WorldMark is a standardized benchmarking toolkit for interactive image-to-video world models. It comprises five components: (i) an Evaluation Dimension Suite of eight metrics spanning Visual Quality, Control Alignment, and World Consistency; (ii) an Image Suite covering diverse scenes (nature, city, indoor) and viewpoints (first-/third-person); (iii) an Action Suite of 15 trajectories with varying complexity; (iv) a Unified Action Interface that translates a shared WASD+L/R action vocabulary into each model’s native control format; and (v) a modular Evaluation Workflow tying the above components into a four-stage pipeline.

Users may also evaluate with custom metrics on our standardized image–action pairs, ensuring fair cross-model comparison. We introduce each component in turn below.

3.1 Evaluation Dimension Suite

As summarized in table 2, WorldMark evaluates generated videos along three complementary dimensions: Visual Quality assesses per-frame fidelity, Control Alignment measures faithfulness to input actions, and World Consistency captures temporal coherence and 3D plausibility. A key design principle is multi-level coverage: Visual Quality captures frame-level distortions detectable by image quality models; Control Alignment reconstructs 3D camera poses to verify geometric fidelity against ground-truth trajectories; and World Consistency combines geometric reprojection with VLM-based semantic judgment to detect temporal degradation invisible to either method alone. This layered design ensures that a model cannot achieve a high aggregate score without excelling across fundamentally different aspects of generation quality.

Visual Quality. We evaluate per-frame visual fidelity from two perspectives.

Aesthetic Quality. We measure human-perceived aesthetic appeal using the LAION aesthetic predictor LAION-AI (2022), which is trained on large-scale human preference data and captures layout, color harmony, lighting balance, and photo-realism.

Imaging Quality. Complementing subjective aesthetics, we quantify low-level distortions with MUSIQ Ke et al. (2021) trained on the SPAQ Fang et al. (2020) dataset, which detects artifacts such as over-exposure, noise, compression, and blur.

Control Alignment. Beyond visual quality, it is crucial to verify whether the model faithfully obeys input control signals. We measure this through two pose-based metrics.

Translation Error. We evaluate spatial consistency between the generated video and the conditioning camera trajectory. DROID-SLAM Teed and Deng (2021) reconstructs camera poses from the synthesized frames, and we compute the scale-invariant Euclidean distance:

et=‖𝐭gt−s​𝐭‖2e_{t}=\|\mathbf{t}_{\text{gt}}-s\mathbf{t}\|_{2} (1)

where 𝐭gt,𝐭∈ℝ3\mathbf{t}_{\text{gt}},\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} are the ground-truth and estimated camera positions, and ss is the least-squares scale factor. This metric ensures the synthesized scene reflects true camera displacements rather than mere 2D pixel shifts.

Rotation Error. Complementary to translation, we measure orientational alignment via the geodesic angular deviation between predicted and ground-truth rotation matrices:

er=arccos⁡(tr​(𝐑gt​𝐑T)−12)⋅180πe_{r}=\arccos\left(\frac{\text{tr}(\mathbf{R}_{\text{gt}}\mathbf{R}^{T})-1}{2}\right)\cdot\frac{180}{\pi} (2)

where 𝐑gt,𝐑∈S​O​(3)\mathbf{R}_{\text{gt}},\mathbf{R}\in SO(3) are the ground-truth and estimated rotation matrices. Since most evaluated models primarily exhibit yaw-axis motion with negligible roll and pitch, this metric effectively captures heading deviations.

World Consistency. This dimension evaluates the model’s ability to maintain a coherent world over time. We employ two complementary approaches: geometric reconstruction and vision–language model (VLM) judgment Zheng et al. (2023).

Reprojection Error. We assess 3D spatial coherence by running DROID-SLAM Teed and Deng (2021) with its Dense Bundle Adjustment (DBA) layer, which jointly refines camera poses and per-pixel depth. The reprojection error is:

ereproj=1|𝒱|​∑(i,j)∈𝒱‖𝐩i​j∗−Π⁡(𝐏i​j)‖2e_{\text{reproj}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{V}}\left\|\mathbf{p}_{ij}^{*}-\Pi(\mathbf{P}_{ij})\right\|_{2} (3)

where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the set of co-visible pixel pairs, 𝐩i​j∗\mathbf{p}_{ij}^{*} is the observed 2D coordinate, 𝐏i​j\mathbf{P}_{ij} is the reconstructed 3D point, and Π⁡(⋅)\Pi(\cdot) denotes camera projection. A higher ereproje_{\text{reproj}} indicates severe geometric inconsistency, implying that the scene’s 3D structure collapses, morphs, or drifts unnaturally over time. Conversely, a lower score reflects superior spatial coherence and a highly stable 3D geometry throughout the generated video.

State Consistency. We evaluate the spatiotemporal stability of objects—whether their shape, texture, and motion remain continuous. A VLM is prompted with uniformly sampled frames to track primary subjects and detect abrupt mutations or jerky movements, outputting a score reflecting physical consistency.

Content Consistency. This metric penalizes sudden appearance or disappearance of objects, targeting common artifacts such as object hallucination and the “popping effect.” The VLM compares scene elements across consecutive keyframes and scores the frequency and severity of spatiotemporal hallucinations.

Style Consistency. This metric assesses the global visual fidelity and aesthetic uniformity of the generated video, targeting anomalies such as color shifting, unnatural distortions, and fluctuations in the overall artistic or photorealistic style. Given a sequence of uniformly sampled frames, the VLM analyzes global visual characteristics—aesthetic tone, lighting, and color palette—and compares them across the timeline to detect stylistic degradation, ultimately producing a quantitative score of aesthetic stability.

3.2 Image Suite

We curate a compact yet diverse set of 50 reference images from the WorldScore dataset, which aggregates images from multiple existing sources. Starting from their curated pool, we remove duplicates and near-duplicate scenes to maximize visual diversity while keeping the total count practical, given the high inference cost of current interactive models.

Since the source dataset does not distinguish camera perspectives, we treat all original images as first-person views. To enable cross-viewpoint evaluation, we use an image generation model Google DeepMind (2026) to synthesize a corresponding third-person view for each scene (fig. 2), yielding 100 test images in total. The resulting Image Suite spans three scene categories (Nature, City, Indoor), two visual styles (Real, Stylized), and two viewpoints (first-/third-person). The stylized subset covers diverse aesthetics including oil painting, Ukiyo-e, cyberpunk, and Minecraft, ensuring that evaluation is not biased toward photorealistic domains alone.

3.3 Action Suite

Interactive evaluation requires standardized input actions alongside reference images. We define 15 action sequences of increasing complexity (fig. 3): unidirectional translations (actions 1–4), unidirectional rotation (action 5), combined translation-rotation trajectories (actions 9–10), and cyclic or repetitive motions (actions 11, 14). All actions are expressed in a shared vocabulary of WASD movement plus L/R yaw rotation, and translated to each model’s native input format via per-model action-mapping adapters (section 3.4).

To systematically probe models at increasing levels of difficulty, we organize evaluation into three tiers: Easy—single-segment trajectories lasting 20 s (e.g., pure forward motion), testing basic action compliance; Medium—two-segment compositions of 40 s (e.g., forward then rotate), requiring smooth transitions between movement types; and Hard—three-segment sequences of 60 s involving complex patrol routes or 360∘360^{\circ} panoramic rotations, demanding sustained world consistency over long horizons. Combined with the 100 test images from the Image Suite, this yields approximately 500 standardized evaluation cases.

For each reference image, we employ a VLM to select contextually plausible actions from this library. The VLM analyzes the scene to identify physical constraints—for example, lateral obstacles in an enclosed space make prolonged sideways translation implausible (fig. 4)—and retains only feasible trajectories.

3.4 Unified Action Interface

A central challenge in benchmarking interactive world models is that each model consumes actions in a proprietary format (table 3): YUME Mao et al. (2025a) interprets WASD instructions embedded in natural-language captions, HY-World 1.5 Sun et al. (2025) and HY-GameCraft Tang et al. (2025) take structured 6-DoF pose parameters, Genie 3 Google DeepMind (2025b) accepts gamepad-style controls, Matrix-Game He et al. (2025) exposes custom action functions, and Open-Oasis Decart et al. (2024) operates on 25-dimensional continuous action vectors. This heterogeneity has been a primary obstacle to cross-model comparison: even if two models are given “move forward,” the actual input representation differs entirely.

WorldMark resolves this with a unified action interface. We define a shared action vocabulary of six discrete primitives—forward (W), backward (S), strafe-left (A), strafe-right (D), yaw-left (L), and yaw-right (R)—each parameterized by duration. All 15 trajectories in the Action Suite are composed from this vocabulary. For each supported model, we implement an action-mapping adapter that translates the canonical representation into the model’s native format. Because individual models differ in angular velocity and movement speed, the adapters calibrate per-model parameters (step size, yaw rate) so that the intended semantic action is faithfully reproduced. This design ensures that all models receive semantically identical instructions while respecting their architectural constraints. Adding support for a new model requires implementing only a single adapter.

3.5 Evaluation Workflow

The preceding subsections define what to evaluate (Evaluation Dimension Suite), what to show the model (Image Suite), what actions to issue (Action Suite), and how to bridge heterogeneous control interfaces (Unified Action Interface). The Evaluation Workflow specifies how these components compose into a complete, reproducible evaluation run.

Given a target model, the user first performs Image Selection—choosing images by viewpoint, scene category, or visual style, or supplying custom references for which a VLM script automatically infers suitable action sequences. The selected images and actions then pass through Action Mapping, where per-model adapters (section 3.4) translate the shared WASD+L/R vocabulary into the target model’s native control format. With the (text, image, action) triplet constructed, Video Generation runs the model under standardized conditions. Finally, Metric Evaluation scores outputs using the eight-metric suite in table 2. The modular design allows users to plug in custom or third-party metrics (e.g., VBench Huang et al. (2024)) without modifying any other stage.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experiment Setup

Evaluated Models. Six representative open-source and proprietary interactive I2V world models are benchmarked on WorldMark. The five open-source models are YUME 1.5 Mao et al. (2025a), Matrix-Game 2.0 He et al. (2025), HY-World 1.5 Sun et al. (2025), HY-GameCraft Li et al. (2025b); Tang et al. (2025) (abbreviated HY-Game in tables), and Open-Oasis Decart et al. (2024). As a representative closed-source model, we evaluate Google’s Genie 3 Google DeepMind (2025b). For first-person evaluation, all six models are tested. For third-person evaluation, only the three models that natively support third-person viewpoints—Matrix-Game 2.0, HY-World 1.5, and Genie 3—are included.

Test Conditions. The Image Suite comprises 50 reference images, categorized into 25 realistic and 25 stylized domains. For each image, we provide paired first-person and third-person views, along with 5 contextually appropriate action sequences selected by a VLM. We utilize Nano-Banana-2 Google DeepMind (2026) for third-person image generation and Gemini-3.1-Pro Google DeepMind (2025a) as the VLM for both automated action selection and video evaluation. All models receive exactly the same reference images and semantically identical action sequences via our unified action interface (section 3.4). We evaluate on four scenario splits: First-Person Real, First-Person Stylized, Third-Person Real, and Third-Person Stylized.

4.2 Quantitative Evaluation Results

First-Person View Evaluation. tables 4 and 5 present the quantitative comparison of the evaluated models in the First-Person Real and First-Person Stylized scenarios, respectively. In terms of Visual Quality, YUME 1.5 and HY-World 1.5 demonstrate superior performance. Specifically, YUME 1.5 achieves the highest scores in both Aesthetic Quality (56.94) and Imaging Quality (74.36) in the Real scenario, while HY-World 1.5 shows competitive results, notably taking the lead in Aesthetic Quality (58.50) within the Stylized scenario.

Regarding control alignment, the results indicate a divergence in model capabilities. HY-Game exhibits robust translation control, achieving the lowest Translation Error in both Real (0.159) and Stylized (0.116) scenarios, as well as the lowest Rotation Error (0.932) in the Stylized setting. Matrix-Game 2.0 also shows strong rotational alignment in the Real scenario (1.324).

For World Consistency, the closed-source Genie 3 significantly outperforms the open-source baselines across almost all metrics. In both Real and Stylized scenarios, it consistently achieves the best or second-best results in Reprojection Error, State Consistency, Content Consistency, and Style Consistency. Notably, in the stylized scenario (table 5), Genie 3 dominates all four consistency metrics, highlighting its robust capability in maintaining spatial-temporal coherence and stylistic stability over long-horizon generations.

Third-Person View Evaluation. table 6 details the evaluation results for the Third-Person scenarios. Because YUME 1.5, HY-Game, and Open-Oasis lack support for third-person perspective generation, we restrict our comparison to Matrix-Game 2.0, HY-World 1.5, and Genie 3. In these scenarios, HY-World 1.5 establishes a clear advantage in Visual Quality, outperforming the others in both Aesthetic and Imaging Quality across both Real and Stylized domains. HY-World 1.5 also demonstrates strong Control Alignment, particularly in the Real scenario, where it achieves the lowest Translation Error (0.206) and Rotation Error (2.137).

Consistent with the first-person evaluations, Genie 3 maintains its dominance in World Consistency within the third-person perspective. It achieves the highest scores in State, Content, and Style Consistency in both Real and Stylized settings. While HY-World 1.5 shows competitive Reprojection Error in the Stylized scenario (0.713), Genie 3’s overall performance underscores the current advantage of advanced proprietary models in preserving complex world dynamics and temporal consistency during interactive video generation.

Real vs. Stylized. Comparing across visual styles, we observe that stylized scenes slightly improve aesthetic scores for some models (HY-World 1.5: 54.79→\to58.50) but degrade control alignment—HY-World 1.5’s Rotation Error increases from 2.08∘2.08^{\circ} to 4.32∘4.32^{\circ}. This suggests that non-photorealistic textures introduce additional difficulty or that models struggle with out-of-distribution visual styles.

Key Takeaways. Four findings stand out. First, visual quality and world consistency are largely uncorrelated: YUME produces the most appealing frames yet its worlds lack logical coherence, while Genie 3 maintains the most consistent worlds with only moderate frame-level fidelity. Second, strong control alignment does not imply overall quality—HY-Game follows commands precisely but at the cost of visual fidelity, whereas Genie 3 has higher trajectory error yet preserves a globally coherent world. Third, third-person generation exposes severe weaknesses: switching from first- to third-person inflates Matrix-Game 2.0’s rotation error by roughly an order of magnitude (∼20×{\sim}20\times), underscoring the difficulty of maintaining camera control around a visible character. Fourth, domain-specific training does not transfer: Open-Oasis, trained on Minecraft, fails across all metrics on real-world and stylized scenes.

4.3 Qualitative Evaluation Results

fig. 5 illustrates a qualitative comparison demonstrating high and low performance across Visual Quality, Control Alignment, and World Consistency. In the leftmost example, the top video exhibits high visual fidelity, whereas the bottom video suffers from significant visual degradation. In the middle example, given the action input ”R” (camera rotating right), the top video correctly executes the rotational movement; conversely, the bottom video incorrectly translates to the right without the expected change in camera angle. Finally, in the rightmost third-person example, the top video successfully maintains character, background, and stylistic consistency, while the bottom video not only exhibits stylistic shifts but also hallucinates new characters into the scene.

We further validate our metrics through a Human Preference Alignment study involving 20 volunteers who manually ranked 50 sets of first-person videos from the six models. By comparing these human rankings with our automated WorldMark Evaluation scores, we observe a good consistency. Quantitatively, the Spearman’s rank correlation between the two sets of results reaches ρ>0.9.\rho>0.9. This strong alignment is visually evident in fig. 6 : the automated metrics produce line trajectories and model performance hierarchies across Visual Quality, Control Alignment, and World Consistency that are nearly identical to those derived from human preferences.

5 Conclusion

We presented WorldMark, the first standardized benchmark for interactive I2V world models, featuring a unified action interface across six heterogeneous control formats, a 500-case test suite, and a multi-level evaluation toolkit. Our evaluation reveals that visual quality and world consistency are largely uncorrelated, that precise control alignment does not imply overall generation quality, and that third-person generation remains an open challenge, with the worst-case rotation error degrading by nearly an order of magnitude relative to the first-person setting. We release all data and code; adding a new model to WorldMark requires only a single action-mapping adapter.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
